Witches. In literature, witches embody supernatural evil and forbidden power, especially feminine power. Shakespeare's three witches in Macbeth are the canonical representation—agents of fate who speak in riddling prophecy, seduce ambition, and orchestrate tragedy. They challenge straightforward morality by making us ask whether they control destiny or merely speak it, whether they corrupt or merely reveal the darkness already in human hearts.

The weird sisters appear on a heath and prophesy that Macbeth will be king. Their ambiguous language invites him to murder while concealing responsibility for his choices. Witches occupy a liminal space—they are supernatural, able to vanish and conjure spirits, yet embodied and interactive. They are neither divine nor demonic, but a third category operating by different rules. Their prophecies are technically true but misleading. "None of woman born shall harm Macbeth" comes to pass through Birnam Wood coming to Dunsinane—literal truth twisted into false assurance.

Witchcraft in early modern literature reflects anxieties about female autonomy, sexuality, and power. Witches often seduce men into ruin, the temptress witch, or they operate outside patriarchal control, the autonomous witch. In literature they are often associated with marginality—age, childlessness, poverty, deformity. They are excluded from normal society and embody its fears and discontents. Sometimes witches are presented as a collective threat, a secret organization working against Christian order, as in The Tempest or The Crucible.

The brilliance of literary witches lies in how they blur the boundary between manipulation and destiny. Are they powerful agents or merely readers of fate? The ambiguity is their power over the audience. In Macbeth's companion Banquo, we see a different response to the witches' address. And in Prospero, the sorcerer from The Tempest, we see how a masculine magician relates to the witches' art differently—his relationship shaped by legitimacy and gender in ways that illuminate what the witches themselves represent.
